Fork — copy the retired ts-defold .d.ts verbatim as the first-party fixture. Zero fidelity risk (the surface is identical to what shipped), and the provenance moves to the real upstream. Best when the ts-defold binding is already correct and the surface is small and stable, so the manual-maintenance cost is low. Hand-author — write a fresh .d.ts from the library's documentation. Only worth it when the ts-defold binding is wrong or absent and the surface is small enough to author confidently. Keep — leave the library ts-defold-sourced. Correct when the surface is large or churns often, so the manual-maintenance cost outweighs the provenance gain, or when a generated lane is likely to become available. Spent for the current corpus: every library the ts-defold registry once carried has severed and library-targets.json holds "targets": [] (see 5. Cut the library over and validate), so a library reaching this decision today has no ts-defold binding to keep — the real choice is fork versus hand-author. 1. Add a fork to the library's library.json Start with library add, which writes the folder, library.json and reviewed.json from the archive URL: Then add the forks entry to library.json by hand, and vendor the upstream Lua it measures against. library add writes no fork, and when it wrote a recipe.json for a generated module, delete that entry and its source/ files if the fork replaces it. Each library sits in its own folder under the data folder, named for its repository: the URL's last path segment, lowercased, without .git (https://github.com/britzl/defcon is defcon/). The folder pins the library's own upstream repository and ref once — an authored library is the sole maintainer of its namespace, so it carries its own repo/ref rather than the shared vendored commit: | File | Field | Required | What it is | | ---- | ----- | -------- | ---------- | | library.json | repo | yes | The GitHub or Codeberg repository URL, e.g. https://github.com/britzl/defcon. upstream:library-check reads no other host. | | library.json | license | no | SPDX-style license id, surfaced by the library page's provenance block. Defaults to "". | | library.json | refKind | no | "tag" or "commit" when upstream publishes no stable release (GitHub's latest release skips prereleases), so the docs page's adopt step names the pinned archive instead of linking a releases page. Omit it for a repo with releases. | | reviewed.json | ref | yes | The immutable upstream ref to pin. Prefer the newest stable release tag (git ls-remote --tags <repo>) — never invent one. When upstream publishes no tags, pin the current default-branch commit SHA instead; the docs page renders the full SHA as the source ref. | Each forked module is one entry in library.json's forks list: | Field | Required | What it is | | ----- | -------- | ---------- | | authored | yes | Path of the vendored authored/forked .d.ts, relative to the library folder — fork/<moduleId>.d.ts. | | moduleId | yes | The library's runtime require path, dotted (e.g. defcon.console). This is the declare module name inside the vendored .d.ts. | | namespace | yes | The artifact stem — the emitted file is api-doc/<namespace>.json. Either a bare stem (defcon) or the dotted moduleId (orthographic.camera): fork onto the retired module name when it already equals the publish namespace, and reach for a bare stem only when nothing else owns it. The orthographic.camera worked example below settles the choice. | | apiDoc | yes | The site's model output path (api-doc/<namespace>.json). | | fidelity | no | Defaults to fidelity/<namespace>.json. A fork records no fidelity artifact (see below); the field mirrors the sibling lanes for a future hand-authored target that wants one. | | upstreamLua | one of two | Library-folder-relative paths of the vendored upstream .lua this target's surface is measured against. See surface parity. | | parityVerdict | one of two | Why this target vendors no upstream .lua: { "reason": ..., "note": ... }. Mutually exclusive with upstreamLua. | | instanceType | when upstream has methods | The exported interface the fork declares the module's instances with, e.g. BehaviorTree. Required once the vendored upstream defines a function M:name(…) method, which parity measures against that interface's methods; it needs upstreamLua. See surface parity. | A missing required field fails loudly, naming the field, the offending entry and its library.json. So does a folder named other than its repository, a folder without reviewed.json, and a module another library folder already names. upstreamLua and parityVerdict are individually optional but jointly mandatory: every entry declares exactly one. Neither field is in the required list, yet an entry declaring neither — or both — fails the same way, naming the offender. That is deliberate. A target with no declaration would otherwise sit in the config indistinguishable from a measured-and-clean one, so the config cannot express "nobody has looked at this yet"; you either measure the surface or record why you cannot. 2. Vendor the .d.ts and generate the artifacts Put the authored/forked declaration at the authored path. For a fork of a ts-defold binding, that is the ts-defold lane's codemodded output (codemodDeclaration in packages/cli/src/library/sync-library-types.ts) — not the raw ts-defold fixture, which the ts-defold lane type-maps on the way out (hash/url/vmath.vector3 → Hash/Url/Vector3) while the authored lane emits its input verbatim, so forking the fixture would ship upstream's Lua type names and fail the dts-declaration-validity gate. The two forms coincide when the library references no mapped core types (persist), which is why the rule is safe to state unconditionally. For a hand-authored library, it is the declaration you wrote. Either way it must be a declare module '<moduleId>' ambient — the target form the emit passes through unchanged. When the library is a native extension, the declaration also carries / @globalTable / so project imports lower to its runtime global rather than a require (see Module form). Then run this command from the toolchain root: resolve serves the vendored .d.ts with one change: each member upstream documents carries upstream's LuaDoc summary as its doc comment unless the fork's own comment is pinned to that text (see Upstream LuaDoc import). Nothing else is transformed: an authored source is already target-form, so the served types are the vendored types. --api-doc-out makes library check, once its checks pass, run extractApiDoc over that printed declaration under the pinned publish namespace, producing the api-doc/<namespace>.json the /api page renders. A member's @deprecated tag carries through to the page as a Deprecated line, with the tag's own text when it has any — so mark a deprecated member in the fork rather than only saying so in its prose. There is no fetch command — the source is vendored by hand, not snapshotted from a primary source — and no fidelity command: there is no primary source to compare against, and the emit is lossless by construction (see below). 3. Emission fidelity is by construction The generated lanes report a coverage number because a parse can lose type information the original had. An authored .d.ts cannot: the printed declaration is the vendored source plus doc comments, so the go/no-go gate is a forked-vs-printed identity diff on types — what resolve prints, with its comments removed, is identical to the vendored fork/<moduleId>.d.ts with its comments removed. sync-authored-types.test.ts asserts this for every fork, and print-library.test.ts checks the lane dispatch serves that print. No fidelity/ artifact is written. Read that gate narrowly. It proves emission fidelity — both sides of the diff are the toolchain repo's own files, so all it certifies is that the print loses no type relative to the vendored .d.ts. It says nothing about whether the vendored surface matches upstream, and there is no primary source to measure it against — that is what "no structured type source" means. A verbatim fork inherits whatever accuracy the binding it copied already had; a corrected fork (see defsave below) is only as accurate as the manual audit behind it. So pin the corrections with per-library shape assertions in packages/cli/src/library/sync-authored-types.test.ts — the closest thing this lane has to an upstream check. 4. Surface parity against the upstream Lua The previous section holds for types: upstream ships none, so there is nothing to measure a fork's type annotations against. It does not hold for the surface. Upstream Lua declares its member names and its parameter names in plain source, and those are comparable — a fork that never got a member, or that dropped a trailing parameter, is measurable without any type information at all. Opting a target in The upstream path is derived from moduleId: replace the dots with slashes and append .lua, so in.button is in/button.lua and richtext.richtext is richtext/richtext.lua. Fetch that path at the library's pinned ref and vendor it under the library folder's source/upstream/, at the same path it has upstream — so britzl/defold-input at in/button.lua lands at defold-input/source/upstream/in/button.lua. Vendor only the module file the target names, never the whole repository: the digest map is per-file, and an unused copy is dead weight the pin still has to defend. The reader accepts two closing forms: a bare return M, and a callable module's return setmetatable(M, { … }) — on one line or spread over several, as long as it starts at column 0. It refuses a metatable carrying index, and one named by a variable whose keys it cannot see, in both cases throwing rather than parsing. A delegated member never appears at column 0, so parsing anyway would report a short surface as the whole one and raise the target's coverage for it. An indented return setmetatable(instance, { … }) inside a factory function is not the module's close and is ignored, which is what the column-0 rule buys. The reader also reads the entries of the returned table's constructor: a column-0 local M = { whose entries run over the following lines gives each top-level name = value entry as a member, a function(…) value as a callable one, so this constructor counts Client as M.Client = Client would: A constructor that closes on its opening line, local M = { NAME = "admob" }, is read too. A nested table's keys stay out. An entry it cannot name — a bracketed ["key"] or a positional value — or entries written on an opening line whose constructor continues past it throw, for the same reason a delegating metatable does. A class module's column-0 function M:name(…) methods are read as well, each with its named parameters and without the implicit self. Parity keys them <instanceType>:<name> and compares them with the methods of the interface the entry names as its instanceType, so a missing or short method costs callable coverage like any other member. The self-index M.index = M that makes the module a class adds no member. A column-0 colon method on any other table throws, since its instances are reached through nothing the reader sees, and so does a name defined both as a method and as a . member. List the vendored paths in upstreamLua, then regenerate: That writes fidelity/authored/<namespace>.json per measured target. Both halves of the upstream surface are compared, on two axes reported side by side. The declared side of each is the fork's api-doc/<namespace>.json — the surface the /api page renders, so the report measures what a reader actually sees. Only the fork's own members are compared. An api-doc element marked global: true is a file-scope name the library installs into the environment, defined upstream in files the target does not vendor, so it is a member of no module and enters neither axis — calling one a phantom would describe real upstream API as invented. declaredGlobals records how many were set aside: 30 for deftest, whose telescope assertions are ambient, and 87 for boom, which declares one module member beside its whole ambient game API. The callable axis, upstream members carrying a parameter list against api-doc FUNCTION elements: | Field | What it counts | | ----- | -------------- | | upstreamMembers | Callable members the upstream module defines. | | declaredGlobals | Declared names the fork installs into the environment rather than onto the module. Counted, never compared. | | declaredMembers | Functions the fork declares. | | missingMembers | Upstream members the fork does not declare at all. | | phantomMembers | Declared members upstream does not have. | | arityMismatches | Shared names whose parameter counts disagree, each with both numbers — the fork's being the widest signature it declares. Names are not compared — a fork may rename parameters freely. | | undocumentedMembers | Upstream prose that reached neither the fork nor the import — a member whose accepted block carries no summary to lower, being nothing but tags or nothing but the member's own name. | | importedDocs | Declared elements carrying upstream's own doc, its summary or only its parameter and return docs, because the fork supplied none or did not pin its own. Counted on both axes. | | refusedDocBlocks | Refused upstream blocks the fork left unanswered — neither documented in the fork's own words nor excused by a recorded parityException. Counted on both axes, and the one term that reports prose the import never saw. Authoring the brief clears the charge. | | refusedDocBlocksTotal | The raw refusal count, before the answered and excused ones are subtracted. Kept so a refusedDocBlocks of 0 cannot be misread as upstream writing no ---only blocks. | | variadicMembers | Shared members compared against a floor rather than an exact count, upstream being variadic. | | overloadedMembers | Shared members the fork declares as several overloads, so the comparison had a set of counts to accept rather than one. | | placeholderMembers | Shared members whose upstream definition ends in a bare with no ... after it, dropped before the counts were compared. | | callableCoverage | Fraction of upstream members that are declared and agree on arity. | An upstream definition ending in ... has no fixed parameter count to disagree with, so function M.play(...) is compared against its named parameters as a floor: the fork must declare at least them, and anything beyond is the rest. variadicMembers says how many shared members that weaker check covered, so a callableCoverage of 1 over a variadic surface cannot be read as fully verified. A fork may also declare one name as several overloads, modelling an upstream body that branches on whether an argument was passed — monarch.transitions.gui.create declares create(node) and create() against upstream's single M.create(node) and its if node then branch. That is a set of call shapes, and the member agrees when any one of them meets the rule above; reading a single count would charge a correct fork for whichever overload the api-doc happened to list last. A disagreement is still reported as one number, the widest shape the fork offers. overloadedMembers counts every member compared that way, for the same reason variadicMembers exists: agreeing because one shape matched is a weaker result than agreeing outright. A generated module can also end a definition in a bare that no body reads and no doc comment describes — nakama.lua opens "Code generated by codegen/generate-rest.go" and 66 of its exports end that way. A trailing discard is not a parameter a consumer can pass meaningfully, so charging the fork for omitting it would report the instrument's defect as the fork's. It is dropped before the counts are compared, and only when it is last: a upstream names in the middle still has to be passed for the parameters after it to land. A written before a ... tail is last only in appearance — a caller fills that slot for any vararg to land — so it is still charged. placeholderMembers counts every member the drop covered, whether or not it changed the verdict. The drop is not merely subtractive — a fork that declared the discard as a real parameter disagrees once it is gone, which is how create_protobuf_any was found declaring a second parameter upstream does not take. The field axis, upstream constants (M.SOME_CONSTANT = "X") against api-doc VARIABLE elements. A TYPEDEF is a type rather than a runtime member and enters neither axis: | Field | What it counts | | ----- | -------------- | | upstreamFields | Non-callable members the upstream module defines. | | declaredFields | Non-callable members the fork declares. | | missingFields | Upstream constants the fork does not declare — values its users cannot reach. | | phantomFields | Declared constants upstream has in neither half — names the fork invented. | | fieldCoverage | Fraction of upstream fields the fork declares. | A name that is callable on either side belongs to the callable axis and is never also counted as a field, so one defect is never charged twice. A fork that declared an upstream function as a constant of a callable type would otherwise be charged on both axes at once — once as a missing member, once as a phantom field — and the second charge would describe an upstream name as invented. No measured target produces the shape today, the one that did having since been corrected, so the rule stands on the classifier rather than on any corpus case. floors in the library's library.json ratchets both axes per module, keyed by moduleId as { "callable": 1, "field": 1 }, each against its own floor: either may rise, neither may fall. A regeneration that lowers either number reds the gate, a floor entry that names only one axis is rejected when the library is read rather than leaving the other unratcheted, and library check measures the fork against the same floors. A non-empty missingMembers, phantomMembers, arityMismatches, missingFields, or phantomFields is a correction to make in the fork — never a number to re-baseline. The measurement exists so the gap stays visible while it is being closed; the current numbers are the honest starting point, not a target. The vendored .lua copies are SHA-256-pinned for the same reason: re-vendoring at a different upstream ref would change what every committed number means without changing the number, so the pin must break loudly and the reports be re-measured rather than the digest updated. nakama is the worked example and the rollout's closing statement: its fork declared 166 functions against upstream's 156 with only 4 agreeing on arity — the corpus's worst case, and the last target to reach a full callableCoverage. Closing it took every kind of correction this page describes. Requests upstream had flattened into positional parameters were still declared as a body table, so a caller following the fork passed a table where upstream reads a string. 84 exports ended in retry_policy, cancellation_token the fork declared nowhere, and the two types that pair with them — cancel and cancellation_token — were themselves among the 16 members it never declared. 26 declared names were not on this module at all, the realtime socket surface among them: the pinned nakama.lua requires that module privately and exposes it only through create_socket. Eleven of the 26 have a counterpart on nakama.socket, now vendored as a target of its own; the other fifteen — thirteen message constructors, a stream-presence listener and a request constructor upstream no longer generates — match neither module at the pin and were phantoms on an older nakama-defold. The field axis then closed on the same terms: all 12 of upstream's enum constants are declared, so both axes read 1. boom is the opposite shape: it declares one of the six members boom/boom.lua defines, the other five being the final/init/on_input/ on_message/update lifecycle hooks boom.script calls rather than API a user writes. Those five are justified rather than missing — see below — so the target reports callableCoverage: 1 with no fork edit at all. Read that beside declaredGlobals: nearly the whole library reaches its users as ambient globals, which this axis does not measure. Corrected or justified Some divergences are not defects. When upstream's own source says a member is not for consumers, declaring it would widen the published surface with a function nobody should call — so the fork is right to omit it, and the report should say so rather than charge it as a gap. parityExceptions in the library's library.json is where that is recorded. It maps each fork's namespace to an array of { name, kind, reason } entries sorted by name. An excepted member counts as correct, is absent from missingMembers, and appears in the artifact's parityExceptions carrying its reason — so a target that reached 1 by justification reads differently from one that reached 1 by declaring everything. kind is a closed set, in the same shape as parityVerdict's reason: | kind | When it applies | | ------ | --------------- | | script-lifecycle | Upstream exports the member for the library's own bundled .script and says so in its own comment. boom's five hooks carry -- called from boom.script; orthographic.camera's init, final and update say "called automatically from … the camera.script" in LuaDoc. | | deprecated-stub | Upstream's body is nothing but error("… is deprecated"), so the member cannot succeed if called. orthographic.camera keeps ten such one-line stubs; six are excepted here. | reason must cite upstream's file and line, so the entry can be re-checked against the pin instead of taken on trust. An arity or phantom exception is deliberately not expressible — no kind is added before a real case asks for one. An entry cannot outlive the defect it justifies. Three throws enforce that, each naming the offending entry: an unknown kind, rejected at parse time; an entry naming a member the pinned upstream does not define — the member was renamed or removed, and the entry is stale; an entry for a member the fork does declare — the exception is unnecessary and must be deleted rather than left to rot. The ledger is not a way to skip a correction. It is the other half of correct it or justify it, and every entry is a claim about upstream that the next reader can check. Upstream LuaDoc import A measured target's printed declaration does not stop at the fork. Where upstream documents a module-level member and the fork does not override it with a pinned comment, upstream's own LuaDoc summary, parameter docs and return docs are printed as that member's doc comment, so a project's editor shows them on hover. The api-doc is lowered from the same printed declaration, so the /api page shows the same text, marked so a reader can tell it apart from the fork's own prose. Six rules bound it: Parameter and return docs follow the declared signature. The summary ends at the first line starting with @. Each @param or @tparam text prints as an @param on every declaration that lists that parameter, in the declaration's order, so an overload carries only its own; @return or @treturn text prints as @returns unless the declaration returns void, and a constant takes no tags. Types never print: a ---@param line is read as LuaLS (name type description), every other line as LDoc (name description, a (type) or a @tparam type dropped), and a following line that opens no tag continues the text. A tag with no description, a vararg ..., and a dotted table field such as config.dsn print nothing. An @ after a space, such as LDoc's @{name} reference, prints as \@ so TypeScript reads it as text rather than as a tag. One blank line inside a comment run does not end the block. Upstream often wraps a long @param list around a blank line, which would otherwise truncate the block to its tag half and lose the summary above it. The blank is crossed only when the segment touching the definition opens no --- block of its own, so a blank-separated section header above a documented member never merges into it, and only ever one blank is crossed. A brief never restates its own symbol. Where upstream writes the member's name as the block's first line and the summary beneath it, the name line is dropped, so the rendered brief is the summary rather than the symbol you are already reading. A first line that merely mentions the name is prose and survives; a block that is only the name imports nothing at all. Fork prose wins only while pinned. A member upstream documents keeps exactly what the fork wrote, on every overload, only while the fork's comment carries an @upstreamDoc pin matching upstream's current text (see Pinning a fork comment); a pinned comment replaces upstream's tags as well as its summary. Without a pin, or with a stale one, upstream's summary, parameter docs and return docs replace the fork's summary and its @param and @returns tags; every other tag, such as @noSelf or @deprecated, stays. A member upstream does not document keeps the fork's comment, pinned or not. A comment holding only tags, such as / @noSelf /, is not a summary: the print puts upstream's doc at the top of that same block, and an @param or @returns the fork wrote there keeps its slot. Only the module's own members. The merge fills the functions and constants directly inside the declare module block. A file-scope global and a member of a nested namespace keep whatever the fork wrote. The import is printed, never vendored. fork/<moduleId>.d.ts is untouched and the print changes comments only, so the identity diff on types still proves the emit is lossless, imported prose stays distinguishable from the fork's forever after, and an upstream doc change reaches the print with no hand edit. A block whose every segment opens with a plain -- rather than --- is refused, and counted as refusedDocBlocksTotal on the target's parity report. Nothing distinguishes such a block from a section header sitting above a run of constants — monarch's -- transition messages and boom's -- initialize boom are the same shape to any parser — so admitting the class would attach one member's heading to another's documentation. The remedy is to author that member's doc-comment in the fork, where a human makes the judgment and the result correctly renders as first-party. refusedDocBlocks charges only the refusals still unanswered, so the remedy actually clears it: write the brief and the member stops counting. A member the fork deliberately does not declare is excused by its parityException instead — there is no element to hang a brief on, and the ledger already carries a human's reading of that same comment, which is why boom's five lifecycle blocks charge nothing. A merely missingMembers name is not excused: its remedy is declaring it. The raw term is what keeps the refusal itself visible — defmath writes all 36 of its blocks that way and charges none of them, every one being answered in the fork's own words. An imported symbol's /api heading carries a U dot labelled Documentation imported from upstream, beside the G dot an ambient global carries. The page's provenance block already names the repo and ref the text came from. Pinning a fork comment A fork comment on a member upstream documents is an override of upstream's text, so it names the text it replaces. Its last line is @upstreamDoc and a 12-character pin, on a line of its own: The pin is a hash of upstream's whole LuaDoc block for that member, tags included, with whitespace collapsed, so re-indenting or re-wrapping upstream's comment keeps it and changing a word or a @param line does not. The pin never prints: the line is removed from the served declaration and the /api page. library check names every fork comment that prints upstream's doc instead, with the pin that would keep it: A notice never fails the check, so an update whose upstream edits a doc you override still lands; it prints upstream's new text until you read it, then either copy the pin into the fork's comment or delete the comment when upstream now says it well. A pin on a member upstream does not document guards nothing and is named as well. A pin shaped any other way, or placed anywhere but a module function's or constant's doc comment, stops the module from printing. Why the two axes are never averaged Neither number is "the" coverage of a target, and no single figure replaces them. A module can agree completely on one axis while missing the other entirely, so folding them into one mean would let each mask the other — exactly the reading the split exists to prevent. platypus is the worked case. It defines one module function and 14 constants, so its callableCoverage is 1 over a single comparison while its fieldCoverage is 1 over fourteen. Both read the same, and they are not the same result: one is a single create agreeing on arity, the other is fourteen constants each found by name. Averaged into one figure the module would look uniformly verified, and the single number would move by a fourteenth for a defect on either side — which is why the two are reported separately whether they agree or not. Read the two together. A perfect callableCoverage over a handful of functions still says nothing about a large upstreamFields, and a perfect fieldCoverage says nothing about arity. A phantom on either axis enters no coverage figure, having no upstream member to be a fraction of, so it is visible only in its list. When a target cannot be measured Record a parityVerdict instead of an empty upstreamLua. The reason comes from a closed set — an unknown one throws, naming the entry — and the note must say what was actually looked at: | reason | When it applies | | -------- | --------------- | | unresolved-path | The moduleId-derived path does not resolve at the pinned ref, including a repository that no longer exists there. No corpus target carries this verdict. Before recording it, check whether the upstream merely moved — an account rename usually redirects, and the same history may be reachable under a new owner. If it is genuinely gone, prefer dropping the library over shipping types nobody can obtain a runtime for. | | no-module-file | Upstream resolves, but declares no single module file this target could be measured against. | | unparseable-shape | The module file exists but closes in a way the reader refuses — a metatable carrying index, or one it cannot read the keys of, either of which could delegate members no column-0 scan would find. No corpus target carries this verdict: boom.boom and in.accelerometer once did, and were lifted into measurement when the reader learned the return setmetatable(M, { call = … }) form they close with. | A verdict is a recorded finding, not a way to skip the work. It says someone looked and what stopped them, which is exactly what an absent declaration cannot say. The corpus currently carries no verdict of any kind — all 35 targets are measured — so every reason above is described rather than exemplified. 5. Cut the library over and validate Severing ts-defold for the library is the same single-module cutover the generated lanes use: Drop the library's row from library-targets.json and its dir from library-classification.json, and delete the retired fixtures/ts-defold/<moduleId>.d.ts. Its api-doc/<moduleId>.json golden is deleted only when the fork publishes under a different namespace; when namespace === moduleId it is instead overwritten in place by the command above. The namespace now resolves to your authored artifacts. Add a usage/<library>-usage.test-d.ts compile proof in the library folder, moving any hand-written block for the old dotted specifier into it. library check type-checks every .ts file under a library's usage/ under skipLibCheck: false together with every module resolve prints, the fork among them. The ts-defold registry is now empty: every library it once carried has severed, so library-targets.json holds "targets": []. The file stays committed anyway — the CLI's registry loader treats a missing file as "no vendored libraries at all" and would drop the LuaLS, script_api and authored lanes with it, and library-classification.json pins its commit against that source block. The site's fourth maintainedHere loader reads each library's forks, so the namespace becomes authored-here — absent from the ts-defold classification and present in a first-party corpus — and its /api page carries the upstream pin automatically. Then run the gates: Commit the library's library.json and reviewed.json, the vendored fork/<moduleId>.d.ts and its usage/ examples together, along with the config and manifest deletions. The emitted api-doc/ report folder is gitignored here and stays uncommitted. Worked example — defcon.console britzl/defcon is a plain-Lua console library with no .script_api and no ---@ annotations, so it is a Bucket-E authored target. Its ts-defold binding was a correct 24-line single-module surface, and the surface is small and stable — exactly the low-maintenance-cost case the fork path is for. Keeping it ts-defold-sourced would forgo the provenance gain for no real saving; a fresh hand-author would be redundant work when the existing binding is already right. So the decision is fork: copy the retired .d.ts verbatim, sever ts-defold, and pin to the real upstream. The reference defcon/library.json: and defcon/reviewed.json pins { "ref": "2.6.0" }. authored vendors the fork; moduleId defcon.console names the declare module a consumer imports; namespace defcon is the single-segment artifact stem, so the golden is api-doc/defcon.json — not the dotted moduleId — keeping the docs Libraries tree and file layout uniform with the other bare-stem severed libraries. Nothing else owned defcon, so it was free to take; orthographic.camera below is the case where it is not. The defcon page then attributes to britzl/defcon at 2.6.0, not the ts-defold/library corpus. Worked example — deftest.deftest britzl/deftest (a test runner, pinned to 2.8.0) is a second fork with the same reference-entry shape as defcon.console. It illustrates one wrinkle: its .d.ts declares ambient top-level globals (describe, before, after, test, assert) alongside declare module 'deftest.deftest'. A fork copies the surface verbatim, so those globals carry into the printed declaration and therefore into the dts-declaration-validity gate's compilation. That is fine — they raise no duplicate-identifier clash — and the api-doc lowering publishes them alongside the module's exports (add, run), each marked as an ambient global so the reference page distinguishes what the import reaches from what is callable without it. Do not alter a vendored fork to suppress such globals; they are part of the library's real surface. A file-scope type is held to a stricter rule than a file-scope value: it publishes only when a published signature names it and it carries members (an interface, or a type alias over an object literal). A union, a function type, or an internal generic helper stays off the page, so a fork's incidental type machinery does not become reference content. Worked example — defmath.defmath subsoap/defmath (a pure-Lua math-helper module) is a third fork with the same reference-entry shape, illustrating the no-tag case: upstream publishes no git tags, so ref pins the default-branch commit SHA (c67c227322334056cea7a631f3ddcdf2bcfd480c) rather than a semver tag. The defmath page attributes to that SHA and its sourceUrl points at .../tree/c67c2273… — expected, not a defect. Its surface also references core engine types: upstream writes them as vmath.vector3 | vmath.vector4 / vmath.quaternion, but the fork — like every vendored declaration in this package — carries the core-type-renamed ambient Vector3 | Vector4 / Quaternion. These resolve in library check, which compiles every fork against the engine types the CLI ships, so a fork consuming engine types needs no special wiring. Worked example — defsave.defsave subsoap/defsave (a save/load helper, pinned to the v1.2.6 tag) is the first fork to correct a surface rather than re-home it: the ts-defold binding declared 7 of upstream's 14 functions and just one of its 16 config fields (appname), and three of the seven returned the wrong type. Neither pure option fits — keep fails the cost model (upstream is frozen and the surface is tiny) and a fork alone would knowingly re-home a half-missing surface, while a full hand-author would rewrite five declarations that are already right (four correct functions plus appname). So fork first, then hand-correct against the pin: copy the retired .d.ts, add the missing members, and fix the wrong signatures reading upstream's Lua as the authority. Extending a fork is gate-safe: the identity diff compares the printed declaration to the vendored fixture, not to the retired ts-defold surface. But that diff proves emission fidelity only — the print loses nothing relative to the vendored .d.ts; it does not check the vendored surface against upstream. That accuracy rests on the manual audit against defsave.lua at the pin plus the per-library shape assertions in packages/cli/src/library/sync-authored-types.test.ts, so correcting a fork moves the accuracy burden onto the author, not onto a gate. Narrowing a wrong return is a breaking change for consumers and belongs in the changelog's ### Breaking section; a types package's value is accuracy, so do not keep a declaration you can see is wrong. Two limits are worth knowing before you correct a surface. Upstream Lua that falls off the end of a function returns nil, so a predicate like defsave's key_exists is boolean | undefined, not boolean — read every branch, not just the explicit returns. And a module's export let fields are still read-only through a consumer's import as ns, so a compile proof pins their types by reading them; there is no way to prove assignability through a namespace import. Worked example — persist.persist whiteboxdev/library-defold-persist (a save/load helper, pinned to the b37f6104… commit SHA since upstream publishes no tags) is the first fork to arrive here from a markdown no-go rather than from having no documented source at all. Its README documents all six functions by name but no parameters and no returns, so the markdown gate scored signature-loss and refused the cutover. That verdict retired the README as a regeneration path — and nothing more. Running the cost model on the still-open maintenance question gives fork: the ts-defold surface is five fully-typed functions in 34 lines, upstream is abandoned (its README redirects to a successor project) so the surface cannot churn, and the recorded loss was the README's, not the .d.ts's. So the cutover itself was verbatim — the identity diff made fidelity 100% by construction, and it shipped no type change at all. The later and separately-auditable edit that anticipated has since landed: the fork now also declares exists, the sixth function upstream's Lua defines and ts-defold never had. Severing does not erase the markdown verdict. persist's no-go/signature-loss record and its README snapshot stay exactly as recorded, and the gate still re-derives the decision on every run — it just compares against the vendored fork instead of the deleted fixtures/ts-defold/ snapshot. That is sound because the comparison is re-derived against whatever the fork now declares, not against an identity: adding exists moved two name-set terms and left the no-go/signature-loss decision exactly where it was. Keeping a dead library-targets.json row alive to feed that lookup would have been the wrong fix: it would make the file stop meaning still ts-defold-sourced, which is the signal the remaining Bucket-C libraries are measured against. Worked example — orthographic.camera britzl/defold-orthographic (a camera suite, pinned to tag 3.6.3) is a second markdown no-go that answered fork, and it settles two questions persist's surface never raised. Which namespace does the fork publish under? persist took the bare persist. orthographic cannot: it is the markdown lane's one registered target, so api-doc/orthographic.json is already a committed regeneration proof owned by that lane, and the no-go hides the bare orthographic namespace from page enumeration. Forking under it would overwrite the proofs and render no page. So the authored target keeps the dotted orthographic.camera — the nakama.engine.defold shape — which takes over the retired ts-defold module name and leaves the route and import string byte-identical. The rule generalizes: when the retired module name already equals the publish namespace, fork onto it; only reach for a bare namespace when nothing else owns it. Which file do you copy? The ts-defold lane runs a type-mapping pass, so fixtures/ts-defold/orthographic.camera.d.ts says hash/url/vmath.vector3 while the codemodded output says Hash/Url/Vector3. persist's two forms were identical, so the template never had to choose. Copy the codemodded output — the authored lane emits its input verbatim, so forking the raw fixture would ship ts-defold's upstream type names and fail the declaration-validity gate. Forking the codemodded output makes the cutover a byte-for-byte no-op, which is what lets you prove the severance and any type correction as two separate diffs. orthographic then took that second diff: upstream documents follow as accepting one game object or a table of them, and the ts-defold binding typed only the singular target: Hash | Url. On a file the toolchain repo now owns, widening it to targets: Hash | Url | (Hash | Url)[] is a one-line edit plus a re-emit. It moves no recorded gate number — the fidelity comparison scores member names, the unknown token, parameter count, return void-ness, and optionality, and a rename plus a union widening touches none of them. The third diff is the signature correction, and unlike the second it does move name sets. The fork gained get_automatic_zoom and set_automatic_zoom (live API upstream defines and ts-defold never had), lost add_projector, get_projection_id and use_projector (deprecated stubs whose upstream body only error()s), and world_to_screen narrowed to the (camera_id, world) upstream actually reads — its third adjust_mode argument was silently ignored at runtime, so narrowing it is breaking on purpose. With nine ledger entries covering the withdrawn stubs and the three camera.script lifecycle hooks, the target reaches callableCoverage: 1. The markdown verdict is re-derived over the new export list and lands on the same no-go. The fourth diff is the field correction, which moves the constants half of that same list: MSG_SET_AUTOMATIC_ZOOM was declared from the pinned camera.lua, and MSG_USE_PROJECTION and ORTHOGRAPHIC_RENDER_SCRIPT_USED were deleted, upstream defining neither anywhere — reading either returned nil, so the deletion is breaking on paper only. The verdict is re-derived a second time and holds: the nineteen constants and five functions the README's API table does not cover are still the surface loss that drove it.

title: Authoring LuaLS library types
text: Authoring LuaLS library types Some pure-Lua Defold libraries ship their own type information as inline LuaLS (---@) annotations rather than a .script_api. This toolchain prints TypeScript declarations for them from those annotations, so a consumer that declares the library gets autocomplete and tsc coverage with no hand-written .d.ts. resolve prints the declaration into the consumer's project from the library version it depends on, or from the sources pinned in library data. Adding such a library is data, not code: you add one entry to the luals list of the library's recipe.json, in its folder under the library data folder (the newest version-named folder under packages/library-types/data/; the library folder also holds the fetched sources under source/), run the three generation commands, check the emitted API-doc description, and commit the library's files and its artifacts. There is no pipeline source to touch — the same front-end that produces the druid types produces yours. This page is for library-type authors. Library data lives in the toolchain repo under packages/library-types/data/, so you add or change a library with a pull request there, not to defold-typescript/library-data. If you only want to use a vendored library in your own game, you need nothing here — just declare the dependency and run resolve. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root. Each tool reads and writes the library data under packages/library-types/data/ and writes its reports to api-doc/ and fidelity/ in packages/library-types/. Is your library a LuaLS target? Two facts decide it: It is plain Lua (installed via Defold's Fetch Libraries, no .script_api), and its source carries inline ---@ annotations — ---@class, ---@field, ---@param, ---@return on the public module. A hand-written library with no annotations is not a LuaLS target; those are maintained as hand-vendored .d.ts forks. A library whose annotations are sparse (near-zero fidelity coverage, see below) will emit a hollow surface and is not worth adding. The library's runtime require path (its moduleId) must not already be claimed by another library in library data — two front-ends emitting the same module would collide. 1. Add a recipe.json entry Start with library add, which writes the folder below from the archive URL, with a starting luals entry and the sources it reads: Then edit recipe.json by hand: add typeRenames and externalTypes for the tokens the library's annotations leave unmapped, narrow sourceGlobs and ignore, and add an entry for each other module the library exposes. The tables below describe every field. Each library pins its own repository and tag — a LuaLS library ships no .d.ts, only annotations, and each lives in its own repo at its own release. Its folder is named for the repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git (https://github.com/Insality/druid is github.com/insality/druid/). The folder pins the library once: | File | Field | Required | What it is | | ---- | ----- | -------- | ---------- | | library.json | repo | yes | The GitHub repository URL, e.g. https://github.com/Insality/druid. | | library.json | license | no | SPDX-style license id, surfaced by the library page's provenance block. Defaults to "". | | library.json | refKind | no | "tag" or "commit" when upstream publishes no stable release (GitHub's latest release skips prereleases), so the docs page's adopt step names the pinned archive instead of linking a releases page. Omit it for a repo with releases. | | reviewed.json | ref | yes | The exact release tag to pin. Resolve the newest stable tag (git ls-remote --tags <repo>) — never invent one. | Each generated module is one entry in recipe.json's luals list: | Field | Required | What it is | | ----- | -------- | ---------- | | sourceGlobs | yes | Globs selecting the .lua files to snapshot, relative to the repo root (e.g. ["druid//.lua"]). | | moduleId | yes | The library's runtime require path, dotted (e.g. druid.druid). This names the emitted declare module and scopes the module-function surface to <moduleId-as-path>.lua. | | namespace | yes | The artifact stem — the emitted files are fidelity/<namespace>.json and api-doc/<namespace>.json. The fetched sources sit under the library folder's source/<namespace>/. | | typeRenames | no | Map from a LuaLS type name to the TypeScript type text to emit (e.g. { "vector3": "Vector3" }). The value is emitted verbatim and may name an ambient global, including a dotted one like debug.FunctionInfo — it never contributes an import. Omit or {} when the library references no renamed types. | | ignore | no | Globs excluded from sourceGlobs — tests, examples, editor widgets. Defaults to []. | | externalTypes | no | Map from a type name another target owns to { "module": "<its moduleId>", "name": "<its export>" } — see below. Omit when the library references no other library's types. | A missing required field fails loudly, naming the field, the offending entry and its recipe.json. Types another library owns A library that requires a second library annotates the borrowed type by its bare name (druid's ---@field on_click event). Left alone that token resolves to nothing local and lowers to unknown. Naming its owner in externalTypes instead makes the emitter write a real import at the top of the declare module block and resolve every use of the token to it: emits import type { event } from 'event.event';, types all 46 of druid's callback fields as event, and resolves the ---@class event.on_size_changed: event parent to a real extends. The import is type-only, so it binds no value and a library that exports a function of the same name (quest.event) still compiles. The key is the LuaLS token as written; module must be the owning target's moduleId exactly, and name its exported type. A token whose local name would collide with one the library declares itself fails loudly rather than silently shadowing it. The consuming project must declare that upstream library too. resolve builds no inter-library dependency graph, so a project that lists druid alone gets druid.druid without event.event — the import then degrades to an error-any under the repo-wide skipLibCheck. Declare both; druid does not run without event.event at runtime either. quest and token import event from event.event the same way (quest also imports queue), so a project that lists either one declares defold-event beside it. Prefer externalTypes over a typeRenames entry pointing at an import(...) type: the api-doc lowering maps through the same context, so an inline import('event.event').event would render as the user-facing signature on the library's /api page, where externalTypes renders the clean event. A runtime require is not by itself a type dependency, so decide from the annotations rather than the requires. panthera opens panthera/panthera.lua with local tweener = require("tweener.tweener"), yet no annotation in its subtree names a tweener type — every easing is annotated string|constant. It therefore takes no externalTypes entry, and a project consuming panthera needs defold-tweener installed for it to run but not for its types to resolve — the inverse of druid, which needs event.event for both. Types the Lua stdlib already owns Some tokens belong to no target at all — the ambient Lua standard library already declares them. log's ---@param debuginfo debuginfo names the table debug.getinfo() returns, which lua-types types as debug.FunctionInfo. That takes a typeRenames entry, not an externalTypes one: The emitted signature reads debuginfo: debug.FunctionInfo with no import line, and the log page renders that same dotted name — the way Vector3 and Opaque<"node"> already render there. The rule: a token another target owns takes externalTypes and gets an import; a token the ambient stdlib already declares takes a dotted typeRenames value and gets none. A library that declares the token itself wins over either, so a rename never shadows a real local declaration. Two naming rules keep such a local declaration from hiding the type a rename names, and both apply with no configuration. An alias that names itself in its own body means the type it shadows: ---@alias hash userdata|hash emits type hash = Opaque<"userdata"> | Hash, and every other hash in the library still names the local alias. A declaration named like a core or typeRenames value is declared with a trailing underscore: ---@alias Url url|string emits type Url = Url | string, the library's own Url references read Url, and an engine url still reads Url. Two declarations that land on one generated name, such as Url beside the library's own Url, fail the emit naming both. Where an upstream annotation restates a member it inherits from such a parent, and restates it incompatibly enough that the emitted redeclaration would not type-check, drop the restatement with an annotationOverrides field override — "fields": { "subscribe": { "drop": true } } — and let the member inherit. Like every override, a drop naming an absent field throws rather than passing silently. The second drop shape is a class-level @overload. The emitter lowers one onto the interface as a call signature, which is right whenever the class really is callable — event's EVENT_METATABLE and PROMISE_METATABLE each carry a real call. It is wrong where the @overload describes the module table while the interface types the instance: log reuses one table as both, but only the module table gets call, and get_logger returns an instance built on { index = M }, which Lua never treats as callable. Drop that signature with "callSignature": { "drop": true } on the interface. Same loud failure as the others: an override naming an interface that has no call signature throws. Some libraries bind a ---@class to a field of the module table instead of declaring a ---@field for it: token writes ---@class token.event.on_token_change: event directly above M.on_token_change = event.create(). The class becomes an interface, but nothing exports the value, so token.on_token_change would not exist in TypeScript. A moduleObject override names the module's class and each bound field with its class: Each field emits as export const on_token_change: token_event_on_token_change;, documented with its class's description, and the module's own class is no longer emitted as an empty interface. The override throws when the module class or a field's type is absent from the model, when the module class already declares the field (upstream added the ---@field, so delete the entry), when a module function has the same name, and when the parser already treats a different class as the module object. Other libraries assign constants to the module table with no annotation at all: live-unbundler writes M.MSG_ALL_LOADED = hash("all_loaded") and M.RES_BOTH = 3 at the top of its module file, so the lane exports neither. A moduleConstants override types each one with a LuaLS token and an optional doc line: Each entry emits as a documented export const MSG_ALL_LOADED: Hash; and appears on the /api page, and its token counts toward the fidelity report like any annotation. Only a column-0 M.NAME = ... on the table the module's own file returns (return M) counts as an assignment, as does the first target of M.DEBUG, M[1] = 1, "DEBUG"; an assignment on another table, such as Other.NAME = 1, does not. The override throws when the returned table never has the name assigned at column 0, when a module function has the same name, and when the module object's class already declares it as a field. A ---@meta file can describe a class's functions with dot syntax: ads-wrapper's ads_networks/ads_network.lua starts with ---@meta, puts ---@class ads_network on local ads_network = { NAME = "ads_network" }, and then annotates function ads_network.setup(params) and its siblings. When the tag is the file's first non-blank line, each such function becomes a method of ads_network declared with this: void (setup(this: void, params?: unknown | undefined): void;), because callers invoke it as network.setup(params), not network:setup(params). In any other file the same form stays a module function, since a runtime module may annotate its own table as a class and still export its functions. A dot function on another local table belongs to that table when the returned module re-exports it at column 0. flow's flow/flex.lua defines function Node.new(opts) on local Node = {}, assigns FL.Node = Node, and ends with return FL, so new is declared on export const Node: { "new"(this: void, ...): Node }, not as a top-level flex.new. Because the file also sets Node.index = Node and Node.new declares ---@return Flow.FlexNode, the Node interface extends Flow_FlexNode, and new plus every method annotated ---@return Flow.FlexNode self return Node, so flex.Node.new({ key: "root" }).set_width(960).calculate_layout(960, 640) keeps the chainable methods. A table exported under several fields is declared under each field. A field assigned more than once declares the table it is assigned last. Where an annotation types a parameter wrongly, a type token on a moduleFunctions parameter replaces it: ads-wrapper's queue.lua writes ---@param fn ads_callback, though run calls fn(network, callback, params), so the ads_wrapper.queue target retypes it: add then emits fn: (network: ads_network, callback: ads_callback, params?: LuaTable) => void. A parameter of interfaces.<name>.methods.<method>.params takes the same type key. Naming an absent function or parameter throws. "optional": true on interfaces.<name>.methods.<method> emits the method as name?(...), for a method the library checks for before it calls it. ads-wrapper's wrapper.lua guards the call with if network.request_idfa then, so the ads_wrapper targets mark ads_network.request_idfa optional, and a network without it still passes ads_wrapper.ads_wrapper.register_network. 2. Generate the artifacts Run the three commands from the toolchain root, in order. Each iterates every LuaLS target in library data, so an unchanged entry re-emits byte-for-byte and only your new entry produces new files. --fetch reads the pinned tree, applies sourceGlobs minus ignore, and writes each selected .lua under <library>/source/<namespace>/, preserving tree shape. This is the only command that touches the network; everything after it reads those committed fixtures, so the pipeline is reproducible offline. --fidelity parses the fixtures and reports how much of the surface resolved to a known type (see below). resolve prints the .d.ts a consumer sees from these fixtures, or from the dependency's own archive. Interfaces and aliases come from the whole snapshot; the module's own functions come only from the moduleId file. --api-doc-out makes library check lower the same model, once its checks pass, to the JSON the /api page renders. A ---@deprecated before a ---@class, ---@alias, or a function declaration carries into both artifacts — as a JSDoc @deprecated in the .d.ts and as a Deprecated line on the /api page, with the tag's own text when it has any. A tag on a type still reaches only the .d.ts, since a type has no page heading of its own to carry the line. Only the strict ---@deprecated form is read; a spaced --- @deprecated is treated as prose, as it is for every other tag. 3. Read the fidelity report fidelity/<namespace>.json tells you whether the emit is worth committing: coverage — the fraction of type tokens that resolved to a known type. Druid sits around 0.9; a healthy new library lands in the same range. Near-zero means the source is not meaningfully annotated — reconsider the target. unknownTokens — the distinct type names that fell back to unknown. A cross- library reference (another Insality module) shows up here until you name its owner in externalTypes, which resolves it; the LuaLS placeholders and a bare ... are not among them, because they declare no type and now lower to unknown without counting against coverage, and neither is a bare function, because it now lowers to the callable type (...args: any[]) => unknown. A rename that should have applied shows up as an unexpected entry — fix typeRenames and re-emit. undocumentedMembers — members with no annotation at all; informational. Each report's coverage is pinned by a committed floor, the module's entry in floors in the library's library.json, so a regeneration that lowers it fails the suite instead of quietly rewriting the report, and library check measures the module against the same floor. Regenerating never touches the floors; when you genuinely improve coverage, lock the win in with which raises each floor to the current coverage and can never lower one. A drop is therefore always a real regression to fix at the source, never a floor to edit down. 4. Check the API-doc description After library check --api-doc-out, open api-doc/<namespace>.json and inspect info.description. It carries the description line on the library's main ---@class. When that class has no description line the value is empty (""), and the /api page renders with no description — the "every library page has a non-empty description" gate fails. Remediate by adding a namespace-keyed entry to <data folder>/library-descriptions.json — "<namespace>": "<one-line summary>", keyed by namespace. The site's fallback in api-surface-loader.ts reads it for LuaLS libraries (a ts-defold library keys its fallback on the upstream classification dir; a LuaLS library has none, so it keys on the namespace directly). druid needs nothing here — its ---@class druid is described, so it never reaches the fallback. decore is the worked example: its ---@class carries no description, its api-doc/decore.json info.description is "", and the committed "decore": "Defold ECS Data Manager" entry supplies the page description. 5. Validate, then commit Run library check over the library data. It runs the reader's checks, prints every module, and type-checks every module resolve prints under skipLibCheck: false, together with each library folder's usage/ examples, so a new target is compiled as soon as its recipe.json lists it; the dts-declaration-validity test runs the same check. Fidelity parity is gated per namespace. Then run the library tests: A brand-new library has no floor entry yet, and the floor gate fails until it gets one — fidelity-floor.ts --raise seeds it at the coverage you just measured. Commit the library's library.json with its floor, reviewed.json and recipe.json and the snapshotted source/<namespace>/ together. Both emitted report folders (fidelity/, api-doc/) are gitignored here and stay uncommitted. Worked example — druid The druid entry is the reference shape: sourceGlobs snapshots the whole druid/ tree; ignore drops its tests and examples; moduleId druid.druid scopes the exported functions to druid/druid.lua while the interfaces merge from every file; typeRenames maps druid's vmath references onto the toolchain's branded Vector types; externalTypes hands druid's callback fields to the event library that owns them. From these fixtures, or from the druid archive a project depends on, resolve prints the declaration it materializes into a consuming project as druid.druid. Libraries that ship a .script_api A native or hybrid library that ships an extension .script_api (the same YAML format every Defold extension ships) has a third ingestion mode, distinct from the LuaLS front-end above: packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts, driven by the scriptApi list of a library's recipe.json. Instead of parsing ---@ annotations, it routes the committed .script_api snapshot through the shared ref-doc emitter — scriptApiToFixtureJson → generateModuleDeclaration, the exact path resolve-time extension typing uses — so one-level nested sub-namespaces (bridge.platform, bridge.achievements) survive into nested namespace blocks. The output is an importable module keyed by moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), matching the LuaLS library goldens, so the library imports under its pinned specifier; the declare global form stays the resolve emitter's, for extensions a project declares. Each entry names scriptApi (the path to the .script_api in the repo), moduleId, namespace, and the exact apiDoc / fidelity output paths; the library folder pins repo and ref as above. The generate arms mirror the LuaLS ones: The first migrated target is Playgama/bridge-defold (pinned v2.3.0), maintained entirely from its .script_api — its former ts-defold binding is gone. Three things are specific to a script_api target and worth knowing: Output paths are pinned explicitly and named for the single-segment namespace. Like the LuaLS libraries, a migrated script_api library is the sole maintainer of its namespace, so its goldens are api-doc/bridge.json and fidelity/bridge.json — not the dotted moduleId — which keeps the docs Libraries tree and the file layout uniform with druid. The require specifier is still the moduleId (declare module 'bridge.bridge'), so resolve prints it under that specifier. Fidelity mirrors the emitter, so an unmapped token counts against coverage. The report is computed over the ref-doc doc with the emitter's own type map: a token the emitter renders as unknown is counted in unknownFallbacks and listed in unknownTokens rather than hidden. A pipe-separated type: or a YAML list (type: [table, string]) is split into one token per alternative before that check, so bridge's string | nil returns resolve to string | undefined and bridge lands at coverage 1. A slot left with no token at all counts as one unknown fallback, listed as (untyped), so it cannot pass as covered. A parameter upstream calls omittable in prose only is declared, not inferred. The .script_api format cannot say that a middle parameter may be left out with the later ones shifting left, and upstream sometimes describes a trailing parameter as optional without marking it optional: true. A target lists either kind of slot under omittableSlots (element, slot, and the upstream evidence that allows it), and the emitted declaration carries two overloads, with and without it. The api-doc page and the fidelity report stay as upstream wrote them. A slot the fixture no longer has fails the emit, so the entry cannot go stale.

title: Refreshing library pins
text: Refreshing library pins Every library whose types the toolchain ships is pinned to one upstream ref in one of five lane registries: the LuaLS, script_api and authored registries, with the fixtures their entries name, sit in the newest data folder, packages/library-types/data/<version>/, and the markdown and OpenAPI registries at the root of packages/library-types/ in a toolchain checkout. Upstream keeps moving; the pins do not. This page is what to do when one of them has fallen behind. Authoring LuaLS library types and Authoring forked library types cover adding a library. This page covers moving one that is already there, which is a different job: the generation commands are the easy half, and the couplings that move with the pin are the half that is not discoverable from the sync scripts. This page is for maintainers of the library data in the toolchain repo, changed by pull requests there. Consuming a library in your own project is resolve, and your project's declared dependency version is unrelated to the pin here. The bun commands on this page run from the toolchain root unless a step names another folder. The library update workflow The Library update workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-update.yml) runs library update over packages/library-types/data/ with the latest CLI, then opens one pull request per library it wrote, from the branch library-update/<library>. It runs daily, and when dispatched: A PR that moves a pin is titled update <library> to <ref>; one that only adds commits to a review is titled record <library> commits. A later run force-pushes the same branch and retitles its open PR, so a library never has two. A library that cannot be read upstream is named in the run's log, and fails the run once every other library has its PR. A run dispatched while another is going waits for it to finish. What merges without a human The workflow turns on auto-merge, so the PR merges once ci-done passes, only when both hold: the change is kept or added, or the PR only records commits; every file the PR touches is the library's reviewed.json or under its source/, and CI scopes it as library data. The second is read from the commit, not from what library update reported, so a file anything else wrote keeps the PR for a human. Every other PR stays open. A run turns off an open PR's auto-merge before it replaces the branch, and turns it on again only for the commit it read. Reading a PR left open The PR body names the change and the members upstream added, removed and changed. A changed PR whose three lists are all empty had no single review of the pinned commit to compare with, so read the diff under source/ instead. The library-check run on the PR says whether the library still fits: a module below its floor is named with the value it measured, and a usage/ proof that stops compiling is named by file and line. Fix the fork, floor or proof as the couplings a re-pin moves with it describe, on a branch of your own: the next run force-pushes library-update/<library> and drops any commit pushed to it. Once yours merges, the next run finds the library current and closes the bot's PR. follows follows in a library's library.json says what library update watches: tags in the pin's series, the default branch, or none. With none set, a library pinned to a commit follows its default branch and any other follows its tags. none holds a library, and no request is made for it. library-defold-persist and library-defold-rendy follow none because their whiteboxdev repos answer 404, which would fail every run; they hold no review, so resolve reports them unrecorded. How a stale pin is noticed The library update workflow runs daily, so a library that moved upstream gets one PR from library-update/<library>, refreshed on each run. The bot closes that PR, with a comment, once a run finds the library current or held, or no longer lists the library, as when a new data folder renames it. The bot files an issue titled library update cannot land <library> only when it cannot land a library: library update failed for it, or its PR's checks were red when the run started. The issue names the failure or links the PR, a later run edits it rather than filing a second, and the bot closes it, with a comment, once neither holds. A run reads the checks before it refreshes any PR, so an issue opens or closes up to one run after the checks finish. bun run upstream:library-check is a manual report that no workflow runs. It scans all five registries and reports, per upstream repo, whether the pin has fallen behind: Three things about the report are worth knowing before you act on it: The unit of work is the repo, not the module. britzl/defold-input backs ten authored modules and britzl/defold-orthographic is consumed by two lanes. One bump answers every dependent, so the check groups by repo + ref, counts the dependents, and lists them under --json. A commit-pinned repo is only actionable when the delta touches a path this repo reads. The registries already record which upstream files each target consumes, so a README-only commit on a pinned repo's default branch reports as behind-head without asking you to do anything. A pin that feeds only the fidelity comparison is marked internal. When every dependent is a markdown or OpenAPI target whose decision is not go, no user receives its output, so the report sets internal and the prose line ends in (internal); the bump needs no changelog bullet. It is still actionable: a stale spec hides upstream movement from the go/no-go comparison. The library update bot does not update these targets, so this report is the only place their drift shows. A repo the check could not read at all is reported as unknown and exits the command non-zero. That is deliberate: a renamed or deleted upstream must not look like "current". The check reads GitHub and Codeberg; a repo on any other host reports unknown. When an upstream moves, search the author's old repos for a pointer to the new home before withdrawing the library. Re-pointing means a new repo and a new ref together, because a moved repo often has rewritten history and the old commit no longer exists there. Survey the Asset Portal The registries only see libraries someone already added. <data folder>/asset-portal.json records every Defold Asset Portal entry, pinned to a defold/asset-portal commit, with the GitHub repo each entry names classified by what a dependency on it installs: The sync refuses to start without GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, because it makes about five API calls per entry. It follows renames, so repo is the canonical URL (the portal's britzl/extension-imgui is recorded as defold/extension-imgui). Each repo is read at its latest release, else its newest tag, else its default-branch head. Files count only inside the repo's game.project [library] include_dirs, since nothing else reaches a project that adds the dependency. Each entry's kind is the first row that matches: | kind | The repo at its pin | | ------ | ------------------- | | no-source | is not readable on GitHub; reason is no-github-url or not-found | | not-a-dependency | declares no include_dirs: a tool, sample or editor integration | | script-api | ships a .script_api, which resolve already types | | native-untyped | ships an ext.manifest without a .script_api | | pure-lua-annotated | ships Lua, and one of up to four sampled files carries ---@ annotations | | pure-lua | ships Lua with no annotated sample | | no-lua-api | ships no Lua: shaders, materials, sounds or editor scripts only | bun run asset-portal:report joins the manifest against every lane registry and the defold org listing in defold-extensions.json, offline, and prints four answers: Tracked: entries whose repo a registry already pins, counted per lane. The portal lane counts the script-api entries that have reference pages. A tracked entry files here whatever its kind. Candidates: untracked entries of kind script-api, native-untyped, pure-lua-annotated or pure-lua that are not archived, not a fork, were pushed within 730 days of the sync, and carry no verdict. They are grouped by kind and ranked by stars, which only order the list and say nothing about quality. Declined: untracked entries with a recorded verdict, each with its reason. Nothing to type: untracked no-lua-api, not-a-dependency and no-source entries. A line between them counts the untracked entries with a Lua API that fail the maintenance rule. After a manifest sync, give every script-api candidate its reference pages: It converts each .script_api under the entry's include_dirs at the pin asset-portal.json recorded, writes the page list to <data folder>/asset-portal-script-api.json and one doc per page under asset-portal-script-api/api-doc/, and rebuilds that directory on every run. Those entries then count as tracked on the portal lane. A doc that fails to convert, a page key another page already holds, or a page key that is not one safe route and file name (ASCII letters, digits, , . and -, starting and ending with a letter, digit or , and not a Windows device name such as CON or NUL before its first .) stops the sync before it changes any file, instead of dropping the page. A page key names only the page's api-doc file: its address comes from the library's origin repo, as Library page addresses describes. A library that moved forge keeps a stale portal entry: the portal's Klaleus/library-defold-checkpoint is gone from GitHub, and the authored lane pins codeberg.org/Klaleus/defold-checkpoint. Map such an entry to the tracked repo in packages/library-types/asset-portal-aliases.json. The report refuses to run when an alias names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or a repo no registry pins. An entry whose pinned tree holds no runtime module a project would require, such as an editor script, an import tool or a project template, stays a candidate until someone looks. Record the decision in packages/library-types/asset-portal-verdicts.json: a map from entry id to one short reason naming what the tree holds instead. A verdict takes the entry off the candidate list for good, whatever its maintenance state. The report refuses to run when a verdict names an entry the manifest no longer lists, or an entry a registry pins directly or through an alias, since either verdict is stale. The weekly Library upstream check workflow (the toolchain's .github/workflows/library-upstream-check.yml) compares the portal head's entry ids with the manifest. When ids were added or removed, it opens one issue, titled Asset portal entries differ from asset-portal.json, that lists them and names the re-sync command. The title never changes, so later runs stay quiet while that issue is open. A changed entry under an unchanged id is not reported, because the portal rewrites release metadata every six hours. Refresh the lane Four lanes fetch and regenerate. Run their commands from the toolchain root, in order, after editing the pinned ref: | Lane | Pin | Commands | | ---- | --- | -------- | | LuaLS | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun run --cwd packages/library-types luals:fetch, then luals:fidelity, api-doc | | Markdown | markdown-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-markdown-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | OpenAPI | openapi-targets.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-openapi-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --api-doc | | script_api | the library folder's reviewed.json | bun packages/cli/src/library/sync-script-api-types.ts --fetch --fidelity --data packages/library-types/data, then bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc | A library folder sits in the newest version-named folder of packages/library-types/data/, named for its repository: its <host>/<owner>/<repo>, lowercased, without .git. --fetch is the only step that touches the network; everything after it reads the committed fixtures, so a regeneration is reproducible offline. No lane writes a declaration: resolve prints each target's types from its fixtures, so check them by printing them with bun test packages/cli/src/library from the toolchain root. Set GITHUB_TOKEN before fetching. The fetchers read it (sync-luals-types.ts and sync-library-types.ts both send it as a bearer token) and GitHub degrades unauthenticated API traffic — the git/trees calls behind --fetch and upstream:library-check can return 504 Gateway Timeout on every attempt while the rate-limit budget still shows requests remaining, so a 504 here is not evidence that the pin or the repo is wrong. The authored lane is the exception, and it is the one that surprises people. A library's forks have no --fetch and no fidelity pass. Their source/upstream/ snapshots are vendored by hand and their .d.ts is hand-written, so bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc is the only command they take. Refreshing an authored pin means: 1. edit the ref in the library folder's reviewed.json; 2. copy the upstream files named by upstreamLua into the library folder's source/upstream/… by hand (the path under it mirrors the upstream path); 3. update the hand-written .d.ts for whatever the new upstream added or changed; 4. re-run bun run --cwd packages/library-types parity and bun run --cwd packages/library-types api-doc. The couplings a re-pin moves with it None of these are visible from the sync scripts, and each of them reds ci if you skip it. The committed floor. floors in the library's library.json holds a per-module measurement the gates and library check assert against. New upstream surface changes the measurement, so the floor entry moves with the pin — raise a generated module's ratio with bun run --cwd packages/library-types fidelity:floor, and edit a fork's or native extension's { callable, field } pair by hand. The vendored-snapshot digest. authored-parity-floor.test.ts pins the SHA-256 of every file under each forked library's source/upstream/, because the committed parity numbers were measured against exactly those bytes. Re-vendoring changes the digest; re-pin it in the same commit, after re-running the parity report and reviewing the coverage change. Never re-baseline a digest to make a red go away — that leaves every committed number standing while silently changing what it is about. The provenance assertions. The toolchain's api-surface-loader.test.ts reads the pin back out of the emitted API-doc metadata and asserts it exactly — for druid, meta.commit is the ref in druid/reviewed.json and meta.sourceUrl is https://github.com/Insality/druid/tree/<ref>. A bump moves both, and they are in a different package from the pin you edited.
